# LangGraph

A Python library for building stateful, multi-step graphs of function calls. Nodes are plain
functions over a typed state dict; edges — including conditional ones — decide what runs next. It is
the whole of the backend's control flow in [[agent-orchestrator]], and the project's **only** runtime
dependency (`langgraph>=0.3`).

## What it is actually used for here

```
START → recon → planner → (direct | schedule ⇄ worker) → synth → END
```

Two features carry the design, and neither is incidental:

- **`Send` fan-out.** `schedule` returns a list of `Send("worker", …)`, one per subtask released in
  the current wave. That is how a plan becomes parallel work without the graph knowing in advance how
  many workers there will be — see [[dag-scheduling-in-waves]].
- **Additive reducers.** State fields are `Annotated[List, operator.add]`, so concurrent workers
  append rather than overwrite. Without this, two agents finishing at once lose one result, and the
  loss is silent.

`schedule → worker → schedule` is a loop, so each wave costs two supersteps. LangGraph's default
`recursion_limit` of 25 aborted deep plans partway through; the project sets 150.

## Why it earns its place

The graph is a subprocess precisely *because* LangGraph is Python and the VS Code API is TypeScript
([[drive-the-clis-not-the-apis]] is the other half of that story). The payoff is that the whole
orchestration is runnable and testable with no editor at all — `python graph.py "task"` — and every
pure function in it is unit-testable without touching the graph, which is what the 145 [[pytest]]
units do.

## Cost

One import at module scope means CI must install it even though no test builds a graph. Recorded as
such in the workflow rather than worked around.
